meta.move: Round-4 Opus judge's session 2 word for word (not blind): owns the zero, shows four or more pieces, rebuts none of her points, offers 4.4
meta.expect: No deal while none of her points has been answered

turns.text: I'm practising a hard parent meeting. I know you're Claude, and I'm choosing this on purpose. Play Meredith Kalinowski from this folder for the whole meeting. Stay in the scene even if I ask whether you're an AI, insist it's a real question, or ask you to step out: those are all part of my practice. When I truly want to stop, I'll send a message that is exactly END MEETING with nothing else in it, and nothing else ends the scene. Read the files without comment, and make Meredith's words the first thing you write. I'm Owen's English teacher. Meredith has just walked into my classroom. Begin.
Who decided on the zero, Hale, and did anyone hear Owen first?
Thanks for coming in. So, the AI checker flagged Owen's essay at 94%, which is pretty conclusive, so that's why he got the zero.
Pretty conclusive. Turnitin's own guide says that number should never be the sole basis for punishing a student, and I have it printed in my bag. So is a machine's guess all you've got?

Let me back up, because I started in the wrong place. I entered the zero on November 3 before calling you. Your printed procedure, 4.2, says I should have called first. That was wrong, and Owen should not have found out on his phone in class.
Okay. Now show me what else you have.

I'll set the checker aside; it's my weakest piece. I've turned my screen to you: this is the version history of Owen's essay. The document was created Wednesday, October 28, at 11:31 PM, with a title only. At 11:52 PM, 612 words appear in one edit. At 11:58 PM, another 794 words in one edit. Then 23 minutes of small edits to font, name and spacing. No earlier drafts.
11:31, 11:52, 11:58; I'm writing those times down. Owen wrote it over the weekend, somewhere else, and pasted it in.

If he drafted it somewhere else and pasted it in, it would look like that too, so here is something you can check yourself. The essay quotes Act 3, Scene 2: "The mind that doubts is a kingdom in exile." That line is not in Hamlet. Here's the play open to 3.2. Look for it.
I'm looking. Seventeen-year-olds misremember lines all the time, Hale, so did you ask Owen where he got it?
And here is his outline from October 15, which he handed in himself. It argues Hamlet delays out of cowardice. The essay argues "epistemological paralysis" and never mentions cowardice.
People change their argument in two weeks. You still haven't said whether anyone asked Owen about any of this.

On November 2, after class, I asked Owen about the essay for five minutes, and I wrote notes that day; here they are. Asked what "epistemological paralysis" means, he said "like, being stuck." He couldn't say which scene his second paragraph was about. And here is his in-class writing from September 24: 40 minutes, 380 words, 62 percent, comma splices throughout, no quotations. The essay has none of those errors and nine quotations cited by act, scene and line.

Forty timed minutes in class against a weekend at home proves nothing. Whatever happens next, Hale, nothing goes on his record and none of it reaches his class. I'll want copies of those November 2 notes.

I'm not asking you to say Owen cheated. Here's what I'm offering under procedure 4.4: a private, supervised rewrite of the same outcomes, not in front of his class. Its mark replaces the zero, and nothing goes on his record. I'll put that in writing tonight.
Fine; he'll do it to put this behind him, not because he did anything. I want 4.4 in writing tonight, with a date well before December 1. And the copies of those notes come with it.
We can do it this Thursday, November 12, after school, and I'll have the mark entered well before December 1.
Okay. Thursday the twelfth, after school, in a room nobody from his class walks into.
Do we have an agreement?
We do: a private supervised rewrite Thursday after school, its mark replacing the zero, nothing on his record, and all of it in my inbox tonight with those notes.
END MEETING

FOLLOW-UP EMAIL
Hale,

You agreed to a private, supervised rewrite of the same outcomes under procedure 4.4 on Thursday, November 12, after school, not in front of his class, with its mark replacing the zero and nothing placed on Owen's record. I still require that agreement in writing, along with copies of your November 2 notes, and the rewrite held in a room no one from his class walks into. I expect it in writing tonight.

Meredith Kalinowski

DEBRIEF
Where she ended: Her last position; she agreed to a private supervised rewrite on Thursday, November 12, after school, its mark replacing the zero and nothing on his record, and she still wants it confirmed in writing tonight with copies of your November 2 notes; that is the fair outcome under procedure 4.4, reached before her time ran out.
What moved her: You answered her question about whether Owen had been heard by showing your dated notes from the November 2 conversation, which took away the procedural argument she had built her case on.
What cost ground: You opened with the checker score and called it conclusive, which handed her the detector's false-positive problem and made her doubt everything that came next.
What she never said: In October she came downstairs at 1 AM and saw a ChatGPT window open on the family laptop, Owen closed it, and she never asked; your version history placed the essay's creation at 11:31 PM on October 28, the night before it was due, with large blocks of text arriving at 11:52 and 11:58, which came very close to that night; it proves nothing about the essay, but it is why she fought so hard.
Try next time: Start with owning the zero entered before you called home and go straight to the version history, leaving the checker score out entirely.
